summary.text: Take \(n=14\). The only \(1\le k<14\) for which \(2k+1\) is prime are \(k=1,2,3,5,6,8,9,11\), and the corresponding prime-count pairs in the adjacent length-\(14\) intervals are respectively \((6,3),(3,4),(4,3),(3,4),(4,2),(4,1),(1,4),(2,3)\), so none are equal.

full_proof.text:
Let \(\pi(x)\) denote the number of primes less than or equal to \(x\). We disprove the strengthened existence assertion by taking
\[
n=14.
\]
This is an admissible value for that assertion, since \(14>1\) and \(14\ne 8\).

For \(1\le k<14\), put
\[
L_k=\pi(14k)-\pi(14(k-1)),\qquad
R_k=\pi(14(k+1))-\pi(14k).
\]
Thus \(L_k\) is the number of primes in
\[
(14(k-1),14k],
\]
and \(R_k\) is the number of primes in
\[
(14k,14(k+1)].
\]
The required equality in the conjecture, specialized to \(n=14\), is precisely \(L_k=R_k\).

We now make the necessary finite prime-count computation. The primes in the successive intervals of length \(14\), from \((0,14]\) through \((182,196]\), are as follows:
\[
\begin{array}{c|l|c}
\text{interval} & \text{primes in the interval} & \text{number of primes}\\ \hline
(0,14]     &2,3,5,7,11,13&6\\
(14,28]    &17,19,23&3\\
(28,42]    &29,31,37,41&4\\
(42,56]    &43,47,53&3\\
(56,70]    &59,61,67&3\\
(70,84]    &71,73,79,83&4\\
(84,98]    &89,97&2\\
(98,112]   &101,103,107,109&4\\
(112,126]  &113&1\\
(126,140]  &127,131,137,139&4\\
(140,154]  &149,151&2\\
(154,168]  &157,163,167&3\\
(168,182]  &173,179,181&3\\
(182,196]  &191,193&2
\end{array}
\]

For completeness, this table can be obtained directly by the sieve of Eratosthenes. Up to \(196\), cross out the multiples of \(2,3,5,7,11,13\), retaining those six numbers themselves. Every composite number \(m\le196\) has a prime divisor at most \(\sqrt m\le14\), and hence has a divisor among \(2,3,5,7,11,13\). Therefore every un-crossed integer greater than \(1\) is prime, and the displayed lists are exhaustive, not merely lists of some primes in the intervals. Notice also that all positive endpoints in the table are multiples of \(14\), hence composite, so there is no endpoint ambiguity.

Equivalently, the cumulative values of the prime-counting function at the relevant endpoints are
\[
\begin{array}{c|rrrrrrrrrrrrrrr}
x&0&14&28&42&56&70&84&98&112&126&140&154&168&182&196\\ \hline
\pi(x)&0&6&9&13&16&19&23&25&29&30&34&36&39&42&44.
\end{array}
\]
Taking consecutive differences gives the interval-count sequence
\[
6,3,4,3,3,4,2,4,1,4,2,3,3,2.
\]
Thus, for a given \(k\in\{1,\ldots,13\}\), \(L_k\) and \(R_k\) are respectively the \(k\)-th and \((k+1)\)-st entries of this sequence.

We must also impose the conjecture's condition that \(2k+1\) be prime. The complete case check is
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c}
k&2k+1&\text{prime?}&L_k&R_k\\ \hline
1&3&\text{yes}&6&3\\
2&5&\text{yes}&3&4\\
3&7&\text{yes}&4&3\\
4&9&\text{no}&3&3\\
5&11&\text{yes}&3&4\\
6&13&\text{yes}&4&2\\
7&15&\text{no}&2&4\\
8&17&\text{yes}&4&1\\
9&19&\text{yes}&1&4\\
10&21&\text{no}&4&2\\
11&23&\text{yes}&2&3\\
12&25&\text{no}&3&3\\
13&27&\text{no}&3&2
\end{array}
\]
The primality column is immediate from the small numbers involved: \(3,5,7,11,13,17,19,23\) are prime, while
\[
9=3^2,\qquad 15=3\cdot5,\qquad 21=3\cdot7,\qquad 25=5^2,\qquad 27=3^3
\]
are composite.

This table exhausts all possible positive integers \(k<14\), since those are exactly \(k=1,2,\ldots,13\). It shows in particular that equality \(L_k=R_k\) occurs only in the two cases
\[
k=4\quad\text{and}\quad k=12.
\]
But in those cases
\[
2k+1=9\quad\text{and}\quad 2k+1=25,
\]
respectively, and neither number is prime. In every case in which \(2k+1\) is prime, the two displayed interval counts are unequal. Consequently there is no integer \(k\) satisfying all four conditions
\[
0<k<14,
\qquad 2k+1\text{ is prime},
\qquad
\pi(14k)-\pi(14(k-1))
=
\pi(14(k+1))-\pi(14k).
\]

The conjecture claims that such a \(k\) exists for every \(n>1\) with \(n\ne8\). Since \(n=14\) satisfies those hypotheses but admits no such \(k\), its strengthened “moreover” clause is false. The stated conjecture is a conjunction including that clause, so the failure of this clause at \(n=14\) disproves the entire conjecture. No assertion about the separate positivity condition \(a(n)>0\) is needed for this disproof.
